mainEntity.name: How long does a dental implant crown typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental implant crowns are durable restorations, but their lifespan varies depending on the materials used, the patient's bite, oral hygiene habits, and whether factors such as bruxism are present. In general, implant crowns may last anywhere from 10 to 25 years or more. The implant fixture itself, when well-maintained and properly integrated, is designed to be a long-term solution. Your dentist will be able to give you a more tailored indication based on your individual circumstances during a clinical review.

mainEntity.name: Will replacing an implant crown be painful?

acceptedAnswer.text: Crown replacement is generally a non-surgical or minimally invasive procedure, particularly for screw-retained crowns. Most patients find it comfortable and straightforward. If any adjustments to the abutment or surrounding tissues are needed, local anaesthetic may be used where appropriate. Your dental team will always discuss what to expect before proceeding and will ensure you are comfortable throughout any procedure.

mainEntity.name: Can I have my implant crown replaced at a different dental practice from where the implant was originally placed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, in many cases this is possible, though there are some important considerations. The treating dentist will need to identify the implant system originally used in order to source compatible components. It can be helpful to bring any records or documentation from your original implant treatment if you are attending a new practice. An experienced implant dentist will be able to assess your implant and advise on the available options.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my implant crown needs replacing or if the implant itself is the issue?

acceptedAnswer.text: This distinction can only be reliably made through a clinical examination, which may include dental X-rays to assess the bone levels and condition of the implant. A loose crown does not automatically mean the implant has failed. Equally, not all discomfort around an implant is related to the crown. If you have any concerns, booking a review with a dental professional is the most reliable way to get an accurate picture of what is happening.

mainEntity.name: Is replacing an implant crown expensive?

acceptedAnswer.text: The cost of implant crown replacement varies depending on the complexity of the case, the materials chosen, and the specific clinical work involved. In many cases, replacing only the crown component is less involved — and therefore less costly — than a full implant replacement. Your dental practice will be able to provide a clear cost breakdown following a clinical assessment and discussion of your options. It is worth asking your practice about any treatment plans or phased payment options that may be available. For more information about dental crowns and restorative treatment options, our website has helpful guidance.

mainEntity.name: Does the NHS cover implant crown replacement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental implant treatment, including crown replacement, is not routinely available on the NHS for most patients. It is generally provided as a private dental treatment in the United Kingdom. There are some limited exceptions, but these typically apply to specific clinical circumstances, such as certain cases involving trauma or congenital conditions. A private dental practice will be able to advise you clearly on costs and payment options during a consultation.
